ca_needles_kern_river_the.blurb: This part of the western Sierra centers on the Kern River, with trad as the biggest share, then sport and bouldering. Grades are mostly 5.8 to 5.12, thickest at 5.10 and 5.11. The Needles are granite spires on a narrow ridge above the river, known for long, steep, sustained crack lines alongside some face climbing; May through November is the ideal window, though summer can be very hot. Dome Rock, Elephant Knob and Kernville Rock add more trad, the Lower Kern River Canyon and New Directions hold more routes, and Boulder Gulch is the main bouldering area. The Needles are the summer draw, while the other Kern River crags and the Domelands can be climbed year-round.

bc_grand_wall_boulders.blurb: The Grand Wall Boulders sit in forest at the base of the Stawamus Chief in Squamish and make up a maze of many small zones, all bouldering. Squamish boulders are rough, grippy granite that fell from the Chief's walls, and here that means slopers, heel hooks, lip traverses, compression and some slabs and highballs. Problems are usually low, but landings can be rocky and full of roots, so smaller pads help. Grades run from V0 to V12, mostly V0 to V5. The forest is shady and cool, which suits summer sessions and helps on sloper-heavy lines; fall is often the best season for hard sends. Titanic North, Easy Chair, Thighmaster and Viper are among the biggest zones.

ny_new_york_city.blurb: New York City bouldering is urban and almost entirely boulder problems, set in the city's parks on schist. Grades run from V0 to V12, with most of the problems at V0 to V6. Central Park has by far the most, scattered as small outcrops, and the stone there tends to be polished. Fort Tryon, at the northern tip of Manhattan, has rougher, unpolished stone, switchback paths and old stone arches, with views over the Hudson. Marcus Garvey, Inwood Hill, Morningside and St. Nicholas parks add smaller collections. Some problems sit beside busy streets, while others hide in quieter corners of the parks.

wy_laramie_range.blurb: The Laramie Range in southeast Wyoming is mainly granite, with most climbing between about 6,000 and 7,000 feet. The rock is described as smoother than nearby Vedauwoo, with plenty of hand-sized cracks, and a mix of long ridges and peaks. Sport leads the numbers, with a large trad share and only a handful of top-rope, aid and boulder lines. Roped grades are mostly 5.9 to 5.12, centered on 5.10 and 5.11. Most of the climbing is in the Laramie Peak Wildlife Habitat Management Area, with smaller clusters around Laramie Peak itself, Sellers Mountain, and Curtis Gulch and La Bonte Canyon. Laramie Peak, near 10,000 feet, is a landmark seen across the range. Winter offers good weather windows, while summer can be too hot.

co_west_creek.blurb: West Creek is a less-visited corner of the South Platte at about 7,500 feet, where the climbing takes some effort. Trad is the largest share, followed by bouldering and sport, with single-pitch and multi-pitch lines on both bolts and gear. Roped grades span 5.6 to 5.14, centered on 5.9 to 5.12. Thunder Ridge holds about half the climbing, mostly vertical to slightly overhanging face climbing on featured rock with incut edges and chickenheads, and it includes some of the best 5.12 climbing along the Front Range. Its crags mainly face south: Brown Wall and Alligator Lounge bake in winter sun, while For Real Canyon and Wasp Canyon suit summer. Sheep's Nose is a granite dome, and Bird Rock and Down Under add smaller crags. The area is best from spring through fall.

co_rampart_range_road.blurb: Rampart Range Road runs through the South Platte country near Sedalia at about 7,200 feet, and the climbing is spread over a dozen or so crags and boulder fields. Bouldering is the biggest part, mostly V0 to V4, then trad, sport and top-rope. Roped grades are mostly 5.6 to 5.11. The Bigfoots and Rampart Range Bouldering are the largest zones, mostly boulder problems and a few easy top-ropes. Parachute Rock is the main trad crag, with many classics, and Look At Me Wall is mostly sport and top-rope. Jackson Creek is excellent granite, mostly trad on cracks and friction slabs, sometimes with long runouts between bolts, and its routes are generally easier than those at Devil's Head. Scorpio Dome adds trad and sport.
